conceptTag: First customers for a business app
readerTitle: Your first warehouse wants it free. Now what?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (소규모 유통 창고용 재고 앱, 지역 식료품 체인 안의 재고팀) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 업무용 앱의 첫 고객 거래는 '판매'가 아니라 조건을 설계하는 일이다. 누가, 얼마를, 언제까지, 무엇을 대가로 주는지를 정하면 무료 요청도 배움과 매출로 바뀐다.
misconception: 첫 고객은 일단 무료로 들여보내야 하고, 고객이 원하는 기능은 다 만들어 줘야 계약이 된다.

sources.text: 초기 B2B 영업의 일반적 관행 (디자인 파트너, 유료 파일럿, 정가를 명시한 기간 한정 할인)
모든 인물, 회사, 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 정가 월 $300, 디자인 파트너가 월 $150 × 3개월 = $450. 식료품 체인 파일럿 $1,500 (4개 매장, 3개월).
'많은 회사가 관리자에게 소액 구매 승인 권한을 준다'는 일반적 서술입니다. 특정 금액 기준이나 특정 기업 규정을 사실처럼 적지 않았습니다. 게시 전 표현이 과장되지 않았는지 확인하세요.
이 레슨은 SAL-06-04(디자인 파트너)와 SAL-06-05(첫 거래 가격 정하기)만 적용합니다. 해당 개념 레슨의 용어 정의와 표현이 일치하는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: Three warehouses loved the demo. None has paid.
body: Dana built an app that tells small distributors when to reorder stock. It reads their sales and warns them before shelves run empty.
Three warehouse owners nodded through her demo. One said, "Great. We'll try it if it's free." That sentence decides more about Dana's company than any feature she has built.

image.label: Founder showing a tablet app to a warehouse owner between shelves
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 선반이 높은 작은 유통 창고에서 창업자가 태블릿 화면(재고 그래프, 'Reorder soon' 경고)을 보여주고, 작업복 차림의 창고 주인이 팔짱을 끼고 고개를 끄덕임. 실제 로고나 상표 없음.

cards.title: "We'll try it if it's free."
body: Dana plans to charge $300 a month per warehouse. The app works but is rough in places. The owner, Marco, runs a busy food distributor and has real reorder problems.
What should Dana offer?

options.text: Free until the app is polished, then talk about price
options.feedback: Easy yes, but nothing is at stake for Marco. Free users rarely make time for feedback, and "later" pricing talks often never happen.

options.text: Half price for three months, in return for a weekly 20-minute call and a clear goal, with $300 written as the regular price
options.feedback: This is a **design partner** deal priced as a first deal. Marco gets a discount and influence; Dana gets money, steady feedback and a list price on record.

options.text: Full $300 from day one, take it or leave it
options.feedback: It protects the price and tests real demand. But it asks Marco to pay full price for a rough product, and Dana may lose her best learning partner.

cards.title: A design partner is a customer with a job.
body: Marco takes option B. Every Thursday he shows Dana what went wrong. In week two he points out that his staff count stock on paper first. Dana adds a quick count screen.
That is the point of a **design partner**: an early customer who uses the product for real and helps shape it, under agreed terms.
The weekly call and the shared goal (fewer stock-outs) turn a polite "try it" into a working relationship.

cards.title: The price is a test, not just income.
body: Dana's $150 a month is small money. Its value is what it proves. Marco had to get it approved, decide it was worth it, and keep paying.
This is the core of **pricing your first deals**: charge something, write down the regular price, and put an end date on any discount.
When month four arrives, Marco already knows the price is $300. Nobody has to renegotiate from zero.

cards.title: Marco wants a feature only he needs.
body: Marco asks for support for his unusual pallet labels. It would take Dana about three weeks. The other two warehouses she demoed to use standard labels.
What should she do?

options.text: Build it. Keeping the first partner happy comes first
options.feedback: Marco stays happy, but three weeks go into something nobody else will use. Design partners shape the product only where their problem is common.

options.text: Ask the other two warehouses if they have similar problems before deciding
options.feedback: This uses the design partner idea well: treat Marco's request as a clue, then check if it is shared. If it is, build it. If not, offer a simple workaround.

options.text: Say no and remind him the deal covers feedback, not custom work
options.feedback: It protects Dana's time, but a flat no can sour the partnership. Explaining why, and offering a workaround, keeps the trust.

cards.title: Now a team inside a big company calls.
body: Priya leads the inventory team at a regional grocery chain. Four of its stores keep running out of fresh items. She saw Dana's app at a trade event and wants to try it.
The chain has a long buying process for large contracts. But like many companies, it lets a manager approve small purchases from her own budget.
Priya is keen. Her boss doesn't know Dana exists.

image.label: Team lead at a desk with a store map and four highlighted stores
image.brief: 사무실 책상에서 재고팀 리더가 지역 지도를 보고 있고, 매장 아이콘 4개에 빨간 'Out of stock' 표시. 뒤쪽 유리벽 너머 회의실에 임원들이 보임. 실제 슈퍼마켓 로고 없음.

cards.title: How should Dana price Priya's pilot?
body: The goal is a deal Priya can say yes to, and that can grow into the whole chain later.

options.text: Free pilot in four stores, to get a foot in the door
options.feedback: Fast to start, but no budget is spent, so nobody senior has to care. Free pilots inside big companies often end quietly with no next step.

options.text: A $1,500 three-month paid pilot that fits Priya's own budget, with a success goal and the chain-wide price written in
options.feedback: Pricing the first deal to fit her approval limit gets a real yes now. The shared goal makes Priya a design partner who can take results to her boss.

options.text: Quote the full price for all stores and go through formal buying
options.feedback: It aims for the big win, but months of buying process with no proof is a long wait for an early company. Results from four stores make that pitch stronger.

cards.title: Early deals set habits.
body: Discounts without an end date become the price. Custom work without limits turns a product company into a consulting firm.
Too many design partners is also a trap. Dana can serve two or three well. With ten, the weekly calls eat the time she needs to build.
Write the terms down: price, end date, what each side gives, and what success looks like.

cards.title: Turn "try it free" into terms.
body: Used here: **design partners** (early customers who shape the product in return for agreed commitments) and **pricing your first deals** (charge something, show the real price, set an end date).
**Try it today:** for your next early customer, write one line each for price, end date, what they give, and how you'll both judge success.
